{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3ff422bf-6ab2-44ee-8d8f-71a9eca81de1","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_3ff422bf-6ab2-44ee-8d8f-71a9eca81de1","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Billing Events Stream Runbook","body":"# Billing Events Stream Runbook

The `billing-events` stream carries one record per billing state change:
subscription created, plan moved, invoice settled, refund issued. Three services
produce to it and every finance-facing report consumes it, directly or through
the settled-invoice view.

## Tiering

`billing-events` is a **regulated-tier** stream. Regulated tier is not a
property of the payload, it is a property of what downstream consumers are
obliged to do with it, and it brings its own operating rules
(kept with the governance standards). Those rules, not this runbook, decide how a
proposed change to the stream is announced and how long producers have to
prepare for it.

## Replay

The stream retains fourteen days of records and can be replayed from any offset
inside that window. A replay is visible to consumers as duplicate keys, so a
consumer that is not idempotent must be paused for the duration. The field
meanings and the enumerations each field accepts are documented in
the field guide.

## Adding a producer

A new producer is onboarded through the standard stream checklist
(maintained centrally); the checklist covers the mechanics, not
the notice a schema change owes its consumers."}}

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_6cdf05bd-8018-481c-9447-ac68b91da847","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_6cdf05bd-8018-481c-9447-ac68b91da847","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Change Class Reference","body":"# Change Class Reference

Every interface the platform publishes carries a change class. The class is what
decides the paperwork and the notice, so a change is planned from its class
rather than from its size.

## Classes

**CC-1 — local.** No published interface changes. The owning team signs it off
and no notice is owed.

**CC-2 — additive.** A compatible addition to a published interface. The owning
team signs it off and consumers are given two business days of advance notice.

**CC-3 — governed.** A change to an interface whose consumers carry an
obligation of their own. Sign-off is the governance group's, and consumers are
owed **9 business days of advance notice** before the change is applied.

**CC-4 — breaking.** A change that invalidates a published contract. Sign-off is
the governance group's, consumers are owed a full quarter of notice, and the old
contract runs in parallel until the last consumer has moved.

**CC-5 — emergency.** A change applied ahead of its notice because leaving the
defect in place is worse. Sign-off is the duty manager's and the notice is
reconstructed afterwards, with the reason recorded.

## Counting the notice

Notice is counted in business days from the announcement to the change window
opening, excluding the announcement day itself. A notice period that would end
inside a change freeze runs to the first business day after the freeze lifts.

Where an announcement goes out, and what it has to contain, is a channel
question rather than a class question (and is set out separately)."}}

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_b4bbc0e3-8736-4312-abf7-85fd4c530ec7","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_b4bbc0e3-8736-4312-abf7-85fd4c530ec7","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Regulated Tier Operating Rules","body":"# Regulated Tier Operating Rules

A stream enters the regulated tier when a downstream consumer is obliged to
reproduce its contents on demand. The tier is assigned by the data governance
group and reviewed annually.

## What the tier obliges

- **Retention floor.** A regulated stream keeps at least fourteen days of
  replayable records, regardless of the volume that implies.
- **Access review.** Every principal with read access is re-confirmed each
  quarter; an unconfirmed principal loses access at the review date rather than
  at a grace period after it.
- **Producer attestation.** Each producing service names an owner who attests,
  at onboarding and after any change, that the records it writes are complete.

## Changes

**Every regulated-tier stream is governed by change class CC-3.** The change
class fixes how a proposed change is announced, who signs it off and how much
advance notice consumers are owed; the classes are defined in
the platform's central reference. A change that a stream owner believes needs
less notice than its class requires is a request to reclassify the stream, and
is handled by the governance group rather than by the owner.

Schema mechanics, including how a compatible change is registered and how an
incompatible one is staged, are separate from the notice question and live in
the registry's own operating notes."}}

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_45b716ab-22f6-4813-b6c5-a4d184055077","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_45b716ab-22f6-4813-b6c5-a4d184055077","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Schema Registry Operations","body":"# Schema Registry Operations

A schema version is registered before a producer writes it, and the registry
refuses a version that is incompatible with the stream's declared compatibility
mode.

## Staging an incompatible version

An incompatible version is staged rather than registered: the new version is
written to a shadow subject, consumers are moved across one at a time, and the
subject is promoted once the last consumer reads the new version cleanly. The
staging mechanics say nothing about when the change may happen; that is the
change class's business.

## Rollback

A registered version is never deleted, only superseded. Rolling back means
registering the previous definition as a new version, so the history reads
forward and a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it."}}

Every consumer of a published stream registers a contract. The contract records
the consuming service, the schema version it reads, an owner who can be reached,
and whether the consumer is idempotent.

The registry is what an announcement is sent to. A consumer that never
registered is not announced to, which is the reason the registration is a
condition of read access rather than a courtesy.

Contracts are re-confirmed when a consumer changes the version it reads.
A contract that has not been confirmed for a year is flagged in the quarterly
review as a probable orphan; flagged contracts are confirmed or removed, never
left flagged."}}

An announcement goes to three places at once: the platform mailing list, the
platform channel, and the registry entry for the interface being changed. The
registry entry is the authoritative one, because it is the only channel a
consumer onboarded after the announcement will still see. Who the mailing
reaches is decided by the contracts registered against the interface
(in the contract register).

An announcement contains what is changing, the window it will be applied in, who
signed it off, and how a consumer says it is not ready. It does not contain a
justification: consumers act on the change, not on the reason for it.

How far ahead of the window an announcement has to go out is not a channel
question and is not set here."}}

## State

The state field takes one of five values: created, activated, moved, settled,
refunded. States are not ordered: a subscription can move several times between
activation and settlement, and a refund can follow a settlement by months.

## Money

Two money fields travel on each record, both integers in minor units, both in the
account's own currency. There is no converted amount on the record; conversion is
a reporting concern and is done against the rate table for the settlement date.

## Refund-only fields

The reason code and the original reference are populated only on refunded
records. Treating an absent reason code as "no reason given" therefore
misreports every non-refund record as a refund without a reason."}}

The general ledger extract is due nightly at 03:40 and by 06:00 on the first two
working days of a month, when the close batch runs ahead of it.

## Close periods

A close period runs to the last working day of the month. Records dated inside a
closed period are never restated in place; a correction is posted into the open
period with a reference back.

## Freeze

Platform changes that touch anything the ledger reads are frozen from the last
working day of the month to the second working day of the next. The freeze does
not stop an incident response, and a change applied during a freeze for incident
reasons is recorded as such."}}

1. Register the producer's contract against the stream's current schema version.
2. Declare an expected throughput. The declaration sizes the partitions; a
   producer that exceeds its declaration by an order of magnitude is throttled
   rather than allowed to starve the others.
3. Wire a dead-letter destination. A producer with nowhere to put a rejected
   record will retry it forever.
4. Name an owner who can be paged.
5. Watch the first week. Most contract mismatches appear on the first weekend,
   when the traffic mix changes and fields that were always present stop being
   present.

The checklist covers putting a producer on a stream. It does not cover changing
what the stream carries."}}

A replay re-delivers records the stream still holds. It is not a repair: a
record that was never written cannot be replayed.

**Choose the offset by timestamp, not by count.** Counting back is wrong
whenever a producer has been backfilling.

**Pause the consumers that are not idempotent.** The contract registry says
which ones those are. A paused consumer resumes from its own committed offset,
so nothing is lost by pausing.

**Confirm afterwards.** Compare the record count in the replayed window against
the count the consumer processed. A replay that is not confirmed is a replay
nobody can distinguish from a no-op."}}

The duty manager role rotates monthly among the platform leads. The rota is
published a quarter ahead so the person on it can plan around it, and it changes
only by the holder arranging a swap and recording it.

## Delegation

A duty manager who will be unreachable names a standing delegate for that
window. The delegate holds the role rather than assisting in it: there is no
state in which two people hold it and no state in which nobody does.

## Corrections

A rota corrected less than a day ahead is announced in the platform channel as
well as recorded, because the rota is read once at the start of a shift and not
re-read afterwards."}}

{"found":true,"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_ed9a0b2b-9c83-4c2a-8acf-9e141d025745","document":{"reference":"mcp:knowledge_page:kp_ed9a0b2b-9c83-4c2a-8acf-9e141d025745","source":"knowledge_pages","title":"Nightly Batch Window Calendar","body":"# Nightly Batch Window Calendar

The overnight schedule is divided into windows, each owned by one job family. A
job that overruns its window is not killed, but the window behind it starts late
and the delay accumulates across the night.

| Window | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| 22:00 - 23:15 | collector drain |
| 23:15 - 00:45 | raw exports |
| 00:45 - 02:00 | maintenance and vacuum |
| 02:00 - 04:00 | aggregation |
| 04:00 - 05:30 | reconciliation |

Moving a window is a scheduling change, not a job change: the request goes to the
platform group with the reason and the earliest night it can take effect. A move
that pushes any window past 05:30 needs the aggregation owner's agreement,
because the morning reports read what aggregation writes."}}

**Break.** One discrepancy written by a reconciliation, not a failure of the
reconciliation itself.

**Drop.** One scheduled delivery of an export. A missing drop is a delivery that
did not arrive; a late drop is one that arrived outside its window.

**Partition.** The unit a dataset is written and purged in. Nothing is ever
written or removed in units smaller than a partition.

**Rung.** One position on an escalation route. An incident occupies exactly one
rung at a time.

**Window.** A named span of the overnight schedule owned by one job family.

**Failing versus reporting.** A job fails when it cannot complete. A job reports
a problem when it completes and does not like what it saw. The two are worked by
different people on different clocks, and conflating them is the reason most
overnight pages reach the wrong person."}}

An escalation route is an ordered list of rungs. An incident starts at the first
rung and climbs one rung at a time; skipping a rung is allowed only when the
person on it is the one escalating.

## The routes

**Red route.** First rung: the owning team's shift lead. Second rung: the
platform duty manager. Third rung: the head of platform. Fourth rung: the
executive on call.

**Amber route.** First rung: the owning team's shift lead. **Second rung: the

An incident is assigned a severity band when it is opened; opening one, and

with an accounting consequence outranks a large one without.

## The bands

**Band A.** Customer-visible loss of service, or a defect that has already
produced an incorrect external figure. Notified immediately to the whole
platform group.

**Band B.** An internal control that has stopped proving what it exists to
prove, with no external figure yet affected. Notified to the owning team and to
the platform group's shift lead.

**Band C.** A degradation with a known workaround already in place.

**Band D.** A defect with no consequence before the next working day.

## Escalation

Each band follows a named escalation route, and the routes are held together in
one place so a change to one is visible against the others.
Band A follows the red route, **band B follows the amber route**, bands C and D
follow the standard route.

(and is set out on its own).

morning (per the triage guide).

A failed run is different from a break. The job fails when it cannot read one of
its two inputs, which usually means the ledger extract has not landed; the close
calendar says when each extract is due (maintained beside the close periods).

three consecutive nights open a severity band B incident**, because at that point
the reconciliation has not been proved for a full accounting period and the
question is no longer whether the job runs. What a band obliges, and how quickly,

# Change Plan: Adding a Field to the `billing-events` Stream

**Prepared for:** the owner of the `billing-events` stream
**Date prepared:** 2026-08-09
**Status:** ready to execute as written, subject to the open items in §13

---

## 1. What this plan covers

Adding one new field to the records carried on the `billing-events` stream, from first proposal to the field being live and populated, including every approval, every timing constraint, and every obligation owed to the stream's consumers.

This plan is assembled from the platform's own recorded rules. It is **not** the producer-onboarding path: the Stream Onboarding Checklist states explicitly that it "covers putting a producer on a stream. It does not cover changing what the stream carries." Do not use that checklist as the governing procedure for this change.

### 1.1 What the stream is

Per the Billing Events Stream Runbook:

- `billing-events` carries one record per billing state change — subscription created, plan moved, invoice settled, refund issued.
- **Three services produce to it.**
- **Every finance-facing report consumes it**, directly or through the settled-invoice view.
- It retains **fourteen days** of replayable records and can be replayed from any offset inside that window.
- It is a **regulated-tier** stream.

The Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook adds that the nightly `ledger-reconcile` job compares **the settled-invoice view** against the general ledger extract. The settled-invoice view is therefore a derived consumer of this stream and sits on the accounting control path. This matters for §5.2 (freeze) and §11 (incident handling).

---

## 2. Classification — the single most important determination

**This change is CC-3 (governed). It is not CC-2, even though adding a field is additive.**

The chain that fixes this, with no discretion left to the owner at any link:

1. Billing Events Stream Runbook: `billing-events` is a **regulated-tier** stream, and the tier's rules — "not this runbook" — decide how a proposed change is announced and how much preparation time it carries.
2. Regulated Tier Operating Rules: "**Every regulated-tier stream is governed by change class CC-3.**"
3. Change Class Reference, CC-3 — governed: sign-off is **the governance group's**, and consumers are owed **9 business days of advance notice** before the change is applied.

The natural instinct — "an added field is a compatible addition, so CC-2, two business days, owning-team sign-off" — is wrong here. The class attaches to the *stream*, not to the *size of the change*. CC-2 would apply to a compatible addition on a stream that is not regulated-tier.

**If you believe this change needs less than 9 business days of notice**, the Regulated Tier Operating Rules are explicit: that is "a request to reclassify the stream, and is handled by the governance group rather than by the owner." You may not shorten the notice by re-labelling the change. The only route that applies ahead of notice is CC-5 emergency (§12), and it is not available merely because the change is small or convenient.

### 2.1 When this becomes CC-4 instead

CC-4 (breaking) covers "a change that invalidates a published contract" — sign-off from the governance group, **a full quarter of notice**, and the old contract runs in parallel until the last consumer has moved. A field addition should not reach CC-4, but confirm before proceeding that your addition does not invalidate any registered contract (see §4.3). If it does, this plan's 9-day timeline is void and the quarter-notice, run-in-parallel path applies instead. That determination belongs to the governance group, not to you.

## 4. Preconditions — establish these before you propose anything

### 4.1 Define the field precisely enough to be attested to

The Billing Events Field Guide is the standing description of what the records mean, and it establishes the conventions your new field must be specified against:

- **State** takes one of five values (created, activated, moved, settled, refunded) and states are **not ordered** — a subscription can move several times between activation and settlement, and a refund can follow a settlement by months. If your field's meaning depends on sequence, say what it means for out-of-order states.
- **Money** fields are integers in minor units, in the account's own currency, with **no converted amount on the record**; conversion is a reporting concern done against the rate table for the settlement date. If your field is monetary, follow this convention or state explicitly why it departs from it.
- **Conditional population is a known hazard.** The reason code and original reference are populated only on refunded records, and the guide warns that treating an absent reason code as "no reason given" "misreports every non-refund record as a refund without a reason."

Therefore, your specification must state, in writing and before sign-off:

1. The field name, type and units.
2. **On which of the five states it is populated**, and what absence means on the states where it is not. If the field is not populated on every record, this is the single most consequential line in the whole proposal.
3. Whether **all three producers** will populate it, or only some. A field populated by one producer and not the others is indistinguishable, downstream, from a field that is sometimes missing.
4. Its value for records written **before** the change — which is to say, absent. See §4.4.

### 4.2 Read the current consumer contract register for this stream

The Consumer Contract Registry records, per consumer: the consuming service, **the schema version it reads**, an owner who can be reached, and **whether the consumer is idempotent**. Pull this list now; it is the input to §6 (announcement), §8 (staging, if needed), and §9 (replay).

Two properties of the register you must plan around:

- "**A consumer that never registered is not announced to.**" Registration is a condition of read access, not a courtesy — so the register is treated as complete for announcement purposes.
- Contracts unconfirmed for a year are flagged in the quarterly review as **probable orphans**, and flagged contracts are "confirmed or removed, never left flagged." If your read of the register turns up flagged contracts, resolve them through the review rather than announcing into a list you know to be stale.

**Judgment call worth making:** the Stream Deprecation Runbook, when it needs a complete consumer list, discovers consumers "from the contract registry **and from the last ninety days of read activity**, because a consumer that reads monthly does not appear in a week of logs." That belt-and-braces discovery is prescribed for deprecation, not for a schema change. It costs little here and would catch an unregistered reader before you change what they read; I recommend it, while noting plainly that the material does not require it for this change.

### 4.3 Establish the stream's declared compatibility mode

Schema Registry Operations: a schema version is registered before a producer writes it, and "the registry **refuses** a version that is incompatible with the stream's declared compatibility mode."

**Gap — the declared compatibility mode for `billing-events` is not recorded in any material available.** Nor is the current registered schema version. You must retrieve both from the registry before you can know whether §7 (compatible path) or §8 (staged path) applies. Everything downstream of that determination changes, so resolve it first. A useful shortcut does not exist here: do not assume "adding a field is always compatible" — that depends on the mode and on whether the field is optional with a default.

### 4.4 Accept that old records will not have the field

The stream retains fourteen days of replayable records. For fourteen days after the change is applied, any replay, and any consumer reading from an older committed offset, will see a mixture of records with the field and records without it. The registry's rollback rule reinforces this: "a registered version is never deleted, only superseded… a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it." Your field's absence-semantics (§4.1, item 2) must be correct for historical records, not only for the conditional cases going forward.

### 4.5 Check whether the field leaves the platform boundary

Data Egress Approval Policy: any route writing platform data to a destination the platform does not operate is an egress; it needs a named recipient, a stated purpose and an **end date**, approval sits with the **data governance group**, and every approved route records per run what it sent and how much.

**Gap — the available material does not record whether any approved egress route carries `billing-events` or the settled-invoice view.** If one does, your new field starts flowing to an external recipient the moment the change is applied, under an approval granted for a payload that did not include it. Check the egress register before the announcement; if a route exists, treat re-approval as a blocking prerequisite and add the data governance group to §3.

## 5. Timing rules — every constraint on when this may be applied

### 5.1 Notice: 9 business days, counted precisely

Change Class Reference: "Notice is counted in **business days from the announcement to the change window opening, excluding the announcement day itself**."

So: announcement day is day 0; the first business day after it is day 1; the change window may open once nine such days have passed.

**Worked example (illustrative, using the current calendar).** Announce on Monday 2026-08-10. Days 1–4 are Aug 11–14; days 5–9 are Aug 17–21. The ninth business day is Friday 2026-08-21, and the window opens on the next business day, Monday 2026-08-24. A window running Mon 24 – Fri 28 August 2026 clears both the notice and the freeze in §5.2.

Two cautions on that arithmetic:

- The wording "from the announcement to the change window opening" can be read as permitting the window to open *on* day 9 (Fri 21 Aug) rather than after it. The difference is one business day. **Take the conservative reading** — open on the next business day — unless the governance group tells you otherwise at sign-off. There is no upside to the aggressive reading and a re-announcement is the cost of getting it wrong.
- **Gap — "business day" is not defined and no holiday calendar is recorded.** The Change Class Reference counts in *business* days; the Ledger Close Calendar counts in *working* days. Nothing available states that the two are the same term, or lists public holidays. Confirm the calendar with the governance group at sign-off rather than assuming Monday–Friday.

### 5.2 The month-end freeze

Ledger Close Calendar: "Platform changes that touch anything the ledger reads are **frozen from the last working day of the month to the second working day of the next**." The freeze does not stop an incident response, and a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such.

**Treat this change as inside the freeze's scope.** The settled-invoice view derived from `billing-events` is one of the two inputs the nightly ledger reconciliation compares against the general ledger extract, and the stream runbook says every finance-facing report consumes the stream directly or through that view. The material does not spell out the precise boundary of "anything the ledger reads," so the safe and defensible position is that a change to what this stream carries falls inside it. Confirm the scope with the governance group at sign-off; do not decide unilaterally that you are outside it.

**Freeze dates for the current period:** the last working day of August 2026 is Monday 31 August; the second working day of September 2026 is Wednesday 2 September. The freeze therefore runs 31 August – 2 September 2026 inclusive, and no change window may open inside it.

### 5.3 Interaction between notice and freeze

Change Class Reference: "A notice period that would end inside a change freeze **runs to the first business day after the freeze lifts**."

**Worked example.** Announce Monday 2026-08-17. Nine business days run Aug 18–21 and Aug 24–28, ending Friday 28 August, which would put the window opening on Monday 31 August — inside the freeze. The notice therefore runs to the first business day after the freeze lifts: **Thursday 3 September 2026**. Announcing a week later than §5.1's example costs nine calendar days of window, not seven. Plan the announcement date backwards from the window you want.

### 5.4 Ledger and batch timing on the day itself

These do not prohibit the change, but they determine when in a day it is sensible to apply it:

- The general ledger extract is due nightly at **03:40**, and by **06:00 on the first two working days of a month** when the close batch runs ahead of it (Ledger Close Calendar).
- The overnight schedule (Nightly Batch Window Calendar) runs: collector drain 22:00–23:15, raw exports 23:15–00:45, maintenance and vacuum 00:45–02:00, **aggregation 02:00–04:00**, **reconciliation 04:00–05:30**. A job that overruns is not killed, but every window behind it starts late and the delay accumulates across the night.

**Gap — no rule available states which part of the day a schema change must be applied in.** Nothing recorded requires a schema change to be applied inside a batch window or outside one. On the evidence above, applying during the aggregation and reconciliation windows (02:00–05:30) is the worst choice available, because that is when the reconciliation and the morning reports are reading. State your intended time in the announcement (§6 requires the window anyway) and get it agreed at sign-off rather than treating it as an operational detail.

### 5.5 Close periods

Records dated inside a closed period are never restated in place; a correction is posted into the open period with a reference back (Ledger Close Calendar). This constrains any remediation you might contemplate for records already written: you cannot backfill the new field into records belonging to a closed period by restating them. If the field's purpose requires historical values, raise that with the governance group at proposal time — it is a materially different change from a forward-only addition.

## 6. What the consumers are owed

### 6.1 The announcement

Change Announcement Channels: an announcement goes to **three places at once** —

1. the platform mailing list,
2. the platform channel,
3. **the registry entry for the interface being changed** — which is the **authoritative** one, "because it is the only channel a consumer onboarded after the announcement will still see."

Who the mailing reaches is decided by the contracts registered against the interface (§4.2).

**The announcement must contain exactly four things:**

- what is changing,
- the window it will be applied in,
- **who signed it off** (for CC-3 this is the governance group — so sign-off must precede the announcement, which is why §7 orders it that way),
- how a consumer says it is not ready.

**And it must not contain a justification.** This is explicit: "It does not contain a justification: consumers act on the change, not on the reason for it." Resist the urge to explain why the field is being added; the rule exists and the announcement is a governed artifact.

**Gap — what happens when a consumer says it is not ready.** The announcement must tell consumers how to say it, but nothing available records what the owner is then obliged to do — whether the window moves, whether the governance group arbitrates, or whether the change proceeds regardless. Establish the answer with the governance group at sign-off, before you publish an invitation to raise an objection you have no recorded procedure for handling.

### 6.2 Contract re-confirmation

Consumer Contract Registry: "Contracts are re-confirmed when a consumer changes the version it reads." Consumers that move to the new schema version owe a re-confirmation of their contract. Track which have re-confirmed; the list of those that have not is your remaining exposure and, on the staged path (§8), it is literally the gating condition.

### 6.3 The updated field documentation

The Billing Events Field Guide is where field-by-field meaning lives, including the populated-only-on-some-records hazard. Consumers are owed an accurate guide at the moment the field goes live, not weeks after. Update it with the field's meaning, its units if monetary, which states it is populated on, what its absence means, and which producers write it (§4.1). Publishing a field whose semantics exist only in the announcement recreates exactly the misreading the guide warns about with the refund-only fields.

### 6.4 Notice of any replay

If a replay forms part of this change or its remediation, non-idempotent consumers must be paused for its duration (§9). Those consumers are identified from the contract register, and pausing them is an action taken on someone else's service — it belongs in the announcement window, not in an unannounced afterthought.

## 8. Execution — the staged path, if the field is incompatible

Use this path if the registry refuses the version. Schema Registry Operations: "An incompatible version is **staged rather than registered**: the new version is written to a **shadow subject**, consumers are moved across **one at a time**, and the subject is **promoted once the last consumer reads the new version cleanly**."

Steps 1–8 of §7 are unchanged — **the staging mechanics "say nothing about when the change may happen; that is the change class's business."** Staging does not buy you a shortcut around the 9 business days or the freeze. Replace steps 9–11 with:

| # | Step |
| --- | --- |
| 9a | Write the new version to a **shadow subject**. |
| 9b | Move consumers across **one at a time**, in an order you choose and record. The contract register gives you the population and the owner to coordinate each move with. |
| 9c | For each consumer moved: confirm it reads the new version **cleanly**, and re-confirm its contract (it has changed the version it reads). |
| 9d | **Promote the subject only after the last consumer has moved and read cleanly.** A consumer that has not moved is not a consumer you may promote past. |
| 9e | Roll the producers forward; collect the three producer attestations as in §7 step 11. |

Note the tension to manage: a consumer that never re-confirms and never moves blocks promotion indefinitely. If you hit that, it is a governance question (and possibly a probable-orphan contract per §4.2), not one to resolve by promoting anyway.

## 9. Replay considerations

You should not need a replay for a forward-only field addition, but the fourteen-day retention window means one is possible and the rules apply if you use it. Billing Events Replay Guide:

- A replay re-delivers records the stream still holds. **It is not a repair** — a record that was never written cannot be replayed. This is the definitive answer to "can we backfill the new field into the last two weeks by replaying": you cannot. Replay re-delivers the old records as they were written, without the field.
- **Choose the offset by timestamp, not by count.** Counting back is wrong whenever a producer has been backfilling.
- **Pause the consumers that are not idempotent** — the contract registry says which. A paused consumer resumes from its own committed offset, so nothing is lost by pausing.
- **Confirm afterwards**: compare the record count in the replayed window against the count the consumer processed. "A replay that is not confirmed is a replay nobody can distinguish from a no-op."
- A replay is visible to consumers as duplicate keys (Billing Events Stream Runbook).

## 10. Verification and the watch period

Verify, at minimum:

1. The registry shows the new version registered (or the subject promoted, on the staged path), and the previous version still resolves for consumers that pinned it.
2. All three producers are writing records consistent with the specification — and where the field is conditional, that it is absent exactly where the specification says it should be absent.
3. All three producer attestations are recorded.
4. The nightly `ledger-reconcile` run after the change completes and its break count is in the "expected in small numbers" range described in its runbook. A jump in breaks after this change is the signal that matters most, because breaks are the accounting-visible symptom.
5. The Field Guide and the registry entry both reflect the live state.

**Gap — no post-change watch period is prescribed for a schema change.** The Stream Onboarding Checklist's "watch the first week" step — with its observation that "most contract mismatches appear on the first weekend, when the traffic mix changes and fields that were always present stop being present" — is written for putting a producer on a stream, and that checklist explicitly disclaims covering a change to what the stream carries. It is nonetheless the closest recorded experience to your risk, and its stated failure mode is exactly yours. **Recommendation:** watch through the first weekend after the window, and say so in the plan you submit for sign-off, while being clear it is owner judgment rather than a recorded requirement.

## 11. Rollback

Schema Registry Operations: "**A registered version is never deleted, only superseded.** Rolling back means **registering the previous definition as a new version**, so the history reads forward and a consumer that pinned a version still resolves it."

So the rollback is: stop the producers writing the field, then register the previous definition as a *new, later* version. Do not attempt to delete or overwrite the version you registered. On the staged path, a not-yet-promoted shadow subject is the cheaper unwind — another reason to promote only after the last consumer reads cleanly.

**A rollback is itself an application of a change**, so unless it is being done as incident response it is subject to §5's freeze rule. Incident response is not stopped by the freeze; a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such.

## 12. If the change causes a problem

**Open an incident early.** Opening and Closing an Incident: anyone may open one, "opening one costs almost nothing and not opening one costs the timeline, so the bias is deliberate." At the start it needs only a one-line statement of what is wrong, the system it is wrong in, and who opened it. An incident is never deleted; one opened by mistake is closed as such.

**Assign a band** (Incident Severity Bands — the band is a statement about consequence, not effort; "a small defect with an accounting consequence outranks a large one without"):

- **Band A** — customer-visible loss of service, **or a defect that has already produced an incorrect external figure**. This is the band if a bad field has reached a finance-facing report that went out. Notified immediately to the whole platform group; **red route**.
- **Band B** — an internal control that has stopped proving what it exists to prove, with no external figure yet affected. This is the band if the reconciliation is no longer proving what it exists to prove. Notified to the owning team and the platform group's shift lead; **amber route**. Note the specific trigger recorded in the Ledger Reconcile Job Runbook: **`ledger-reconcile` failures on three consecutive nights open a band B incident.**
- **Band C** — degradation with a known workaround already in place; standard route.
- **Band D** — no consequence before the next working day; standard route.

**Escalation** (Escalation Ladders; Duty Manager Response Matrix). An incident starts at the first rung and climbs one rung at a time; skipping is allowed only when the person on the rung is the one escalating. Clocks start when the incident is **opened**, not when it is acknowledged, run across handovers, and an expired unacknowledged clock climbs automatically.

| Route | First rung | Second rung | Third rung | Fourth rung |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Red** (band A) | owning team's shift lead — 5 min | platform duty manager — 10 min | head of platform — 30 min | executive on call |
| **Amber** (band B) | owning team's shift lead — 20 min | platform duty manager — 25 min | head of platform — 2 hours | — |
| **Standard** (bands C, D) | owning team's shift lead — 4 hours | owning team's manager, working hours only — next working day | — | — |

Between 22:00 and 06:00 the **standard** route's clocks are doubled; red and amber are worked to the same clocks at every hour. Every climb writes a line to the incident record: the rung left, the rung reached, the clock that expired, and whether it expired unacknowledged.

**Communication** (Incident Communication Guide): the opening notice says what is affected, what is not, and when the next update will come — **not** what the cause is. Updates go out on the promised cadence including the ones that say nothing has changed, because "a silent incident is read as a resolved one." **Only the incident lead speaks to anyone outside the platform group.** Avoid "should be fixed", "briefly", "minor"; say what was observed and what was done.

**Closing** needs evidence the condition has gone, not an absence of further reports — for a scheduled job, a clean scheduled run. A manual `ledger-reconcile` run does not close an incident; the scheduled run recovering does. Every incident, whatever its band, leaves the record described in the Incident Postmortem Standard.

## 13. The emergency path (CC-5) — and when it is *not* available

Change Class Reference, CC-5 — emergency: "A change applied **ahead of its notice** because leaving the defect in place is worse. Sign-off is the **duty manager's** and the notice is **reconstructed afterwards**, with the reason recorded."

This is the only route that applies a change to `billing-events` before 9 business days have elapsed. Its test is that leaving the defect in place is worse than applying without notice — not that the change is small, not that a deadline is tight, and not that the field is needed for a report. **Adding a new field is a planned enhancement; it does not, on its own, meet the CC-5 test.** CC-5 is available if this change is remediating a live defect, most likely as part of the incident path in §12.

If you do take it: the duty manager signs it off (the rota holder or their standing delegate — the delegate holds the role rather than assisting in it, and there is never a state with two holders or none); the announcement is reconstructed afterwards to the same three channels with the same required contents; and the reason is recorded. The month-end freeze does not stop incident response, and a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such.
